reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an easy AVAX-earning method tied to deploying a contract, transferring about $200 of AVAX, and invoking a flash-loan function. The speaker claims this process increases approximately $200 to $1,775, while the described evidence shows an 11.23 AVAX MetaMask transfer and a later conversion display of about $1,772.85. The contract behavior, recipient, on-chain outcome, and realization of the claimed return are not verified, and a personal-risk disclaimer qualifies the presentation without removing the high-return claim and requested transfer.

citations.quote: How To Earn AVAX Easily Using Flash loans Arbitrage On Metamask Works Perfectly.
have metamask connected to Avalanche Mainnet and have AVAX in your wallet to fund the transaction.
On Deploy, Enter your token details and deploy the contract
Send $200 of Avalanche/AVAX to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Call 'flashloan' function in Remix.

opening.argument: The presentation expressly qualifies its personal result instead of promising that viewers will earn the same amount. The description says, “This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK,” and the video is framed as a method that viewers must assess for themselves. That warning matters: a risky demonstration with an uncertain outcome is materially different from a deceptive guarantee. The title’s claim that the process “Works Perfectly” is promotional wording, but the accompanying risk language directly limits how the result should be understood. The evidence therefore supports a high-risk, non-guaranteed experiment rather than an assurance that every viewer will profit.

citations.quote: This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK.
How To Earn AVAX Easily Using Flash loans Arbitrage On Metamask Works Perfectly.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes the transfer and the displayed result, but those facts do not establish deception. The description expressly warns viewers to act at their own risk, and the narration presents the outcome as the speaker’s own experience, not a guaranteed return for everyone. A risk warning may be imperfect, but it is relevant context that the opposing account underweights.

citations.quote: This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not neutralize the surrounding inducement. The same description calls the method “Working!” and instructs viewers to send funds to a deployed contract, while the speaker celebrates a dramatic increase. “Try it at your own risk” shifts responsibility after presenting the opportunity; it does not show that the claimed mechanism or result is reliable, independently verified, or honestly characterized.

opening.argument: The content is structured as an operational demonstration and educational walkthrough. The speaker says there is “preliminary information” about arbitrage and flash loans, identifies source code, opens Remix, changes the compiler, and explains how the process is supposed to work. The description likewise lays out numbered setup steps, including creating a file, compiling it, deploying it, and connecting MetaMask. That is recognizable technical instruction: viewers are shown a tool workflow and a personal test, not merely handed a passive investment offer. The presence of a financial outcome does not by itself convert a programming demonstration into a scam.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not erase what the tutorial teaches. The material is not just abstract education: it supplies deployment instructions and tells viewers to fund the resulting contract. The claimed personal demonstration is also used to illustrate a large return, so the instructional format and promotional message operate together.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical format is real, but it is not a defense to the financial representation. The tutorial culminates in funding a contract and calling a flash-loan function, and the speaker presents a purported multiplication of the viewer’s input. Showing code and interface clicks does not establish that the contract is safe, that the trade works as claimed, or that the displayed value was realized as profit.

This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK.

opening.argument: The observable transaction is better understood as a user-operated software and trading workflow than as a conventional scam mechanism. The instructions concern MetaMask, Remix, a Solidity contract, and gas for swaps; they do not show a request for passwords, seed phrases, account credentials, recruitment, or downline payments. The description identifies the contract code and the relevant platforms, while the frames show a development interface and wallet activity. Even the proposed return is presented through the speaker’s own transaction sequence, not as a contractual guarantee or a payment schedule. Without evidence of a hidden recipient, credential theft, or guaranteed payout, the record supports risky commerce and experimentation, not a proven scam.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of a password request does not answer the central concern. The alleged mechanism requires sending AVAX to a contract controlled through the presented workflow, and the title makes an easy-earning claim. Whether there is recruitment or credential theft is beside the point when the risk is a funded contract paired with an extraordinary return claim.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing-credential argument narrows scams to one mechanism and ignores the one actually presented. The instructions explicitly direct a viewer to deploy a contract, transfer AVAX into it, and invoke a function, while the result is described as turning about $200 into $1,775. Openly naming tools or linking code does not prove that the recipient, contract behavior, or return is legitimate.
